title: Advanced grammar
summary: Precise, formal and complex structures for confident, accurate English.

lessons.title: Advanced conditionals
lessons.explain: The third conditional talks about unreal situations in the past: if + past perfect, would have + past participle. Other words can replace if: unless (if not), provided that, as long as and in case. Wishes about the past use wish + past perfect.
structures: Third: If I had left earlier, I would have caught the train.
Alternatives: Provided that you pay today, we will deliver tomorrow.
Regret: I wish I had studied more. If only I had known.
positive: If she had asked, I would have helped her.
As long as you arrive on time, we can start.
I wish I had taken the job.
negative: If I had not been ill, I would have gone.
We will not leave unless you are ready.
questions: What would you have done if you had missed the flight?
Would they have come if you had invited them?
reallife: Expressing regret: If I had saved more, I could have bought the flat.
Conditions at work: We will proceed provided that the budget is approved.

mistakes.wrong: If I would have known, I would have told you.
mistakes.right: If I had known, I would have told you.
mistakes.why: Do not use would in the if-clause. Use the past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: I will go unless it doesn't rain.
mistakes.right: I will go unless it rains.
mistakes.why: Unless already means if not, so do not add another negative.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct third conditional.
options: If he had studied, he would have passed.
If he studied, he would have passed.
If he had studied, he would pass.
exercises.why: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

exercises.prompt: I wish I ___ more carefully. (listen; past perfect)
exercises.why: Wish + past perfect for a regret about the past.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'if you do not hurry'?
options: Unless you hurry, you will be late.
Unless you do not hurry, you will be late.
Unless you hurried, you would be late.

exercises.prompt: If they had left earlier, they ___ have missed the bus. (would / will)
exercises.why: Would have + past participle in the result clause.

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I had known, I would have called.
If I would have known, I would have called.
If I knew, I would have called.

assessment.prompt: If she had taken a taxi, she ___ been on time. (would have / would)
Which sentence expresses regret about the past?
options: If only I had gone to the party.
If only I go to the party.
If only I will go to the party.

assessment.prompt: You can borrow my car ___ you drive carefully. (provided that / unless)
Choose the correct sentence.
options: I'll take an umbrella in case it rains.
I'll take an umbrella in case it will rain.
I'll take an umbrella in case it rained tomorrow.

lessons.title: Mixed conditionals
lessons.explain: Mixed conditionals combine a past condition with a present result, or a present condition with a past result. Past condition, present result: if + past perfect, would + base verb. Present condition, past result: if + past simple, would have + past participle.
structures: Past cause, present result: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
Present state, past result: If I were more organised, I would have finished yesterday.
Both clauses can be negative or positive.
positive: If I had taken that job, I would be rich now.
If she were braver, she would have spoken up.
negative: If he had not moved, he would not live here now.
If I were not afraid of flying, I would have gone to Japan.
questions: Would you be happier now if you had stayed there?
If you were not so shy, would you have joined the club?
reallife: Reflecting: If I had learned English earlier, I would speak more confidently today.
Explaining a delay: If the manager were here, he would have approved it yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: If I had met her earlier, I would have been married now.
mistakes.right: If I had met her earlier, I would be married now.
mistakes.why: The result is about now, so use would + base verb, not would have.

mistakes.wrong: If I would be taller, I would have played basketball.
mistakes.right: If I were taller, I would have played basketball.
mistakes.why: Use the past simple (were) in the if-clause, not would.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct mixed conditional (past cause, present result).
options: If I had saved money, I would be richer now.
If I saved money, I would have been richer now.
If I had saved money, I would have been richer now.
exercises.why: The result is about now: would + base verb.

exercises.prompt: If I ___ taller, I would have joined the team. (be)
exercises.why: Present state in the if-clause: past simple.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence has a present result of a past action?
options: If she had left earlier, she would be home now.
If she leaves earlier, she will be home.
If she had left earlier, she would have been home.

exercises.prompt: If I had taken the medicine, I ___ better now. (would feel / would have felt)

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I had listened to her, I wouldn't be in this trouble now.
If I listened to her, I wouldn't be in trouble now.
If I would listen to her, I wouldn't be in trouble now.
assessment.why: Past cause with a present result.

assessment.prompt: If he ___ more careful, he would not have broken it. (be)
assessment.why: A general present quality: past simple.

assessment.prompt: Which sentence is a mixed conditional?
options: If I had gone to bed earlier, I would not be tired now.
If I go to bed early, I will not be tired.
If I had gone to bed earlier, I would not have been tired.

assessment.prompt: If they ___ married, they would have moved abroad. (not / be)
assessment.why: A present state with a past result.

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If she were rich, she would have bought the house.
If she would be rich, she bought the house.
If she is rich, she would have bought the house.
assessment.why: If + past simple, would have + past participle.

lessons.title: Inversion
lessons.explain: Inversion puts the helping verb before the subject, as in a question, for emphasis or formality. It is used after negative adverbs at the start of a sentence (never, rarely, seldom, hardly, not only, no sooner) and in some conditionals (Had I known..., Should you need..., Were he here...).
structures: Negative adverb + helping verb + subject: Never have I seen such a view.
Not only ... but also: Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.
Conditional: Had I known, I would have called. Should you need help, ask.
positive: Rarely do we eat out.
No sooner had we arrived than it started to rain.
Had I known, I would have told you.
negative: Not until yesterday did I understand.
Under no circumstances should you open this door.
questions: Have you ever seen such a beautiful view?
Under what conditions would you accept the offer?
reallife: Formal email: Should you require further information, please contact us.
A speech: Seldom have I felt so proud.

mistakes.wrong: Never I have seen such a thing.
mistakes.right: Never have I seen such a thing.
mistakes.why: After a negative adverb at the start, the helping verb comes before the subject.

mistakes.wrong: Not only she won, but she also broke the record.
mistakes.right: Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.
mistakes.why: Not only at the start requires inversion with did.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Rarely do they argue.
Rarely they argue.
Rarely argue they.

exercises.prompt: Never ___ I seen such a mess. (have / did)
exercises.why: Perfect meaning: have before the subject.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite with inversion: 'If I had known, I would have helped.'
options: Had I known, I would have helped.
I had known, would I have helped.
Did I know, I would have helped.

exercises.prompt: No sooner had she left ___ the phone rang. (than / when)

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Seldom do we see him.
Seldom we see him.
Seldom see we him.

assessment.prompt: Not only ___ he forget, but he was also rude. (did / was)
assessment.why: Not only + did + subject + base verb.

assessment.prompt: Which sentence is formal and correct?
options: Should you need help, please call me.
If you should need help please to call me.
You should need help, call me.
assessment.why: Should you replaces if you should.

assessment.prompt: Hardly ___ we arrived when it started to rain. (had / did)
Which sentence is correct?
options: Under no circumstances should you share your password.
Under no circumstances you should share your password.
Under no circumstances share you should your password.

lessons.title: Cleft sentences
lessons.explain: Cleft sentences split one idea into two parts to emphasise something. An it-cleft is It is/was + focus + that/who + clause. A wh-cleft is What + clause + is/was + focus. They show what is new or important.
structures: It-cleft: It was Maria who solved the problem.
Wh-cleft: What I need is a holiday.
All / The thing: All I want is some peace.
positive: It was last week that I met her.
What surprised me was his honesty.
The person who called was my sister.
negative: It was not the price that bothered me.
What I need is not more work.
questions: Was it Tom who broke the vase?
Is it money that you want?
reallife: Correcting someone: It was Friday we agreed on, not Thursday.
Explaining: What I mean is that we need more time.

mistakes.wrong: It was Maria which solved the problem.
mistakes.right: It was Maria who solved the problem.
mistakes.why: Use who (or that) when the focus is a person.

mistakes.wrong: What I need are a holiday.
mistakes.right: What I need is a holiday.
mistakes.why: The verb after a what-clause is usually singular when the focus is a single thing.

exercises.prompt: Choose the cleft sentence that emphasises the person.
options: It was Sara who called.
Sara called yesterday.
Did Sara call?

exercises.prompt: ___ I like most is the food. (What / It)
Rewrite to stress 'yesterday': 'I saw him yesterday.'
options: It was yesterday that I saw him.
What I saw him was yesterday.
It yesterday was that I saw him.

exercises.prompt: What she wants ___ a quiet life. (is / are)

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: It was the noise that woke me up.
It was the noise what woke me up.
It the noise was that woke me up.

assessment.prompt: What I need ___ a good night's sleep. (is / are)
Which sentence is a wh-cleft?
options: What annoys me is the delay.
The delay annoys me.
It annoys me, the delay.

assessment.prompt: It was my brother ___ taught me to swim. (who / what)
Why do we use cleft sentences?
options: To emphasise one part of the message
To make a sentence negative
To talk about the past only

lessons.title: Subjunctive mood
lessons.explain: The subjunctive expresses wishes, demands, suggestions and unreal situations. After verbs such as suggest, recommend, insist, demand and require, use the base verb for all subjects (that he be, that she go). For unreal wishes and conditions about the present, use were for all subjects (If I were you).
structures: Mandative: I suggest that he see a doctor.
Wish / if + were: I wish she were here. If I were you...
Fixed phrases: Long live the king. So be it.
positive: The manager insisted that she attend the meeting.
I wish it were Friday.
It is essential that he be on time.
negative: I suggest that he not go alone.
It is vital that she not forget.
questions: What do you recommend that I do?
If you were me, what would you choose?
reallife: Formal advice: I recommend that you submit the form today.
Wishing: I wish I were able to help.

mistakes.wrong: I suggest that he sees a doctor.
mistakes.right: I suggest that he see a doctor.
mistakes.why: In the mandative subjunctive, the verb stays in the base form with no -s.

mistakes.wrong: I wish I was taller.
mistakes.right: I wish I were taller.
mistakes.why: In formal English, use were for the subjunctive. Was is common in casual speech.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She demanded that he apologise.
She demanded that he apologises.
She demanded that he apologised.

exercises.prompt: I wish he ___ here now. (be)
Choose the correct sentence.
options: It is important that she be on time.
It is important that she is on time.
It is important that she being on time.

exercises.prompt: The doctor recommended that he ___ more rest. (get)

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I insist that he come with us.
I insist that he comes with us.
I insist that he will come with us.

assessment.prompt: If I ___ you, I would accept. (be)
Which sentence is correct?
options: The rule requires that every student wear a uniform.
The rule requires that every student wears a uniform.
The rule requires that every student to wear a uniform.

assessment.prompt: I suggest that he ___ a doctor. (see / sees)
assessment.why: After suggest that, the verb stays in the base form.

assessment.prompt: Which sentence expresses an unreal wish?
options: I wish I were on holiday.
I hope I am on holiday.
I think I am on holiday.

lessons.title: Advanced modal structures
lessons.explain: Modal perfect forms (modal + have + past participle) talk about the past: must have (strong deduction), might / could have (possibility), can't have (impossible), should have (a criticism or regret), needn't have (it was unnecessary). They are used to guess, to regret and to criticise.
structures: Deduction: He must have left early. She can't have known.
Possibility: They might have got lost.
Regret / criticism: You should have called. I needn't have worried.
positive: She must have forgotten the meeting.
You could have told me earlier.
They might have missed the train.
negative: He can't have seen us.
You shouldn't have shouted.
questions: Could they have taken the wrong road?
Should I have called first?
reallife: Guessing: The lights are off. They must have gone out.
Regret: I should have saved more money.

mistakes.wrong: You should have went home.
mistakes.right: You should have gone home.
mistakes.why: Use the past participle after have.

mistakes.wrong: He must had forgotten.
mistakes.right: He must have forgotten.
mistakes.why: After a modal, use have, not had.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence (strong deduction).
options: He must have missed the bus.
He must missed the bus.
He must has missed the bus.

exercises.prompt: You ___ have called me! I was worried. (should / would)
Which means 'it was not necessary, but I did it'?
options: I needn't have brought a coat.
I mustn't have brought a coat.
I can't have brought a coat.

exercises.prompt: She can't ___ seen us. We were hidden. (have)

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: They might have got lost.
They might had got lost.
They might have get lost.

assessment.prompt: I ___ have locked the door. I can't remember. (might / should)
Which sentence expresses regret?
options: I should have studied more.
I must study more.
I can study more.

assessment.prompt: He ___ have won. He didn't even play! (can't / mustn't)
Which is correct?
options: You shouldn't have said that.
You shouldn't had said that.
You shouldn't have say that.

lessons.title: Reduced relative clauses
lessons.explain: A relative clause can be shortened. Remove the relative pronoun and the verb be: the man who is standing there becomes the man standing there. For passive clauses, use the past participle: the book which was written by her becomes the book written by her. Other active clauses can reduce to -ing.
structures: Active: the people who live here → the people living here.
Passive: the cars that were made in Japan → the cars made in Japan.
With be + adjective or place: the girl who is in the red dress → the girl in the red dress.
positive: The students studying here are from Spain.
The report written by Ana is excellent.
Anyone wanting a ticket should wait outside.
negative: Students not wearing uniforms must go home.
The food not eaten will be thrown away.
questions: Who is the man talking to Sara?
Is that the book recommended by your teacher?
reallife: Notice: Passengers travelling to Delhi should go to gate 4.
Email: The documents attached to this message are confidential.

mistakes.wrong: The man who talking to Sara is my uncle.
mistakes.right: The man talking to Sara is my uncle.
mistakes.why: If you reduce the clause, remove who as well as is.

mistakes.wrong: The letter writing by Tom was long.
mistakes.right: The letter written by Tom was long.
mistakes.why: A passive meaning needs the past participle.

exercises.prompt: Reduce: 'The woman who is sitting there is my aunt.'
options: The woman sitting there is my aunt.
The woman who sitting there is my aunt.
The woman sat there is my aunt.

exercises.prompt: The photos ___ by my father are beautiful. (take)
exercises.why: Past participle for a passive meaning.

exercises.prompt: Which is a reduced clause?
options: The cars made in India are cheap.
The cars which they make in India are cheap.
The cars are made in India.

exercises.prompt: People ___ in the city often use the metro. (live)

assessment.prompt: Reduce: 'The book that was written by Rao is popular.'
options: The book written by Rao is popular.
The book writing by Rao is popular.
The book that written by Rao is popular.

assessment.prompt: The boy ___ at the door is my cousin. (stand)
Which sentence is correct?
options: Students wishing to apply must register.
Students wished to apply must register.
Students who wishing to apply must register.

assessment.prompt: The room ___ for the meeting is small. (book)
Reduce: 'The girl who is in the blue dress is Meena.'
options: The girl in the blue dress is Meena.
The girl is in the blue dress Meena.
The girl who in the blue dress is Meena.

lessons.title: Compound and complex sentences
lessons.explain: Complex sentences combine a main clause with one or more dependent clauses. Using different clause types lets you show reason, contrast, time and extra detail in one sentence. Keep each clause clear, put the most important idea in the main clause, and avoid very long chains.
structures: Main + dependent: I stayed home because I felt ill.
Dependent first: Although it was late, we kept working.
Several clauses: When she arrived, which was after nine, the meeting had already ended.
positive: Although the exam was difficult, most students passed.
The man whom I met yesterday, who works in Pune, offered me a job.
Because the road was closed, we took the train, which was faster.
negative: Although he had not studied, he passed.
I would not have gone if I had known.
questions: Since you were late, did you miss the beginning?
If you could change one thing, which would it be?
reallife: Email: Although we received your request on Monday, we could not reply until today because our system was down.
Opinion: While I agree with you, I think we should wait.

mistakes.wrong: Although he was tired, but he continued.
mistakes.right: Although he was tired, he continued.
mistakes.why: Do not use although and but together.

mistakes.wrong: Because it was raining. We stayed home.
mistakes.right: Because it was raining, we stayed home.
mistakes.why: A dependent clause cannot stand alone as a sentence.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is complex?
options: She left because she was tired.
She left.
She left, and he stayed.
exercises.why: It has a main clause and a dependent clause.

exercises.prompt: ___ he was ill, he went to work. (Although / Because)
Choose the correct sentence.
options: While I was walking, it started to rain.
While I walking, it started to rain.
While walking I, it started rain.

exercises.prompt: Which is NOT a complete sentence?
options: Because she was late.
She was late.
She was late because of the traffic.
exercises.why: Because she was late is only a dependent clause.

assessment.prompt: Choose the best complex sentence.
options: Since the shop was closed, we went home.
Since the shop closed we home went.
Since the shop was closed. We went home.
assessment.why: A dependent clause, a comma, then the main clause.

assessment.prompt: I will call you ___ I get home. (when / but)
Which sentence avoids the error?
options: Although it was cold, we went out.
Although it was cold, but we went out.
Although it was cold, so we went out.

assessment.prompt: The woman ___ lives upstairs is a doctor. (who / which)
assessment.why: A relative clause for a person.

assessment.prompt: Which is a complete sentence?
options: After she finished, she left.
After she finished.
When she left.

lessons.title: Parallelism
lessons.explain: Parallelism means using the same grammatical form for items in a list or pair. If the first item is an -ing form, the others should be -ing forms too. It makes writing clear and balanced. It matters with and, or, not only ... but also, either ... or and comparisons.
structures: List: She likes reading, swimming and cooking.
Pairs: He is not only intelligent but also hardworking.
Correlatives: either to stay or to go.
positive: I enjoy hiking, cycling and swimming.
The job requires patience, creativity and teamwork.
She wants to travel, to learn and to grow.
negative: He neither called nor wrote.
She is not lazy but tired.
questions: Would you rather walk or take a taxi?
Do you prefer reading or watching films?
reallife: CV: Responsible for managing projects, training staff and writing reports.
Instructions: Open the file, check the numbers and save it.

mistakes.wrong: I like swimming, to run and cycling.
mistakes.right: I like swimming, running and cycling.
mistakes.why: Keep the same form (-ing) in the whole list.

mistakes.wrong: She is not only kind but also she works hard.
mistakes.right: She is not only kind but also hardworking.
mistakes.why: Both parts after not only ... but also should have the same structure.

exercises.prompt: Choose the parallel sentence.
options: He likes to read, swim and cook.
He likes to read, swimming and cook.
He likes reading, to swim and cooking.
exercises.why: All three items use to + base verb.

exercises.prompt: She is clever, funny and ___. (kindness / kind)
Choose the correct sentence.
options: Either we leave now or we wait.
Either we leave now or waiting.
Either leaving now or we wait.

exercises.prompt: He neither called nor ___. (write / wrote)
exercises.why: Same past form on both sides.

assessment.prompt: Choose the parallel sentence.
options: The course teaches writing, speaking and listening.
The course teaches writing, to speak and listening.
The course teaches to write, speaking and listen.

assessment.prompt: The manager is firm, fair and ___. (honesty / honest)
Which is correct?
options: She is not only a good singer but also a talented dancer.
She is not only a good singer but also dances talented.
She is not only a good singer but dancing.

assessment.prompt: I would rather stay home than ___ out in the rain. (go / going)
assessment.why: Would rather + base verb ... than + base verb.

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He enjoys fishing, hiking and reading.
He enjoys fishing, to hike and reading.
He enjoys to fish, hiking and read.

lessons.title: Ellipsis and substitution
lessons.explain: Ellipsis means leaving out words that are clear from the context so you do not repeat them: She can swim, and he can [swim] too. Substitution means replacing words with a short word such as one, do, so or not: I like the red one. He said he would help, and he did. Both make speech and writing sound natural.
structures: Ellipsis: I went to the shop and [I] bought milk.
One / ones: Which bag? The blue one.
So / not / do: I think so. I hope not. She passed, and so did he.
positive: I like tea, and my sister does too.
Do you want the large size or the small one?
She said she would come, and she did.
negative: I don't like it, and neither does she.
Is it going to rain? I hope not.
questions: Have you finished? Not yet.
Will he come? I think so.
reallife: Shopping: I'll take the red ones.
Agreeing: I love this song. So do I.

mistakes.wrong: I like it and so I do.
mistakes.right: I like it and so do I.
mistakes.why: After so and neither, the helping verb comes before the subject.

mistakes.wrong: I think not it will rain.
mistakes.right: I don't think it will rain. / I think not.
mistakes.why: Use not as a substitute only at the end of the reply.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct reply: 'I love pizza.'
options: So do I.
So I do.
Do so I.

exercises.prompt: 'I don't like fish.' 'Neither ___ I.' (do / am)
Which word replaces 'bag' in: 'I like the red bag but not the blue bag'?
options: one
it
that
exercises.why: One replaces a singular countable noun.

exercises.prompt: 'Will it rain tomorrow?' 'I hope ___.' (not / no)

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct reply: 'She can't swim.'
options: Neither can I.
Neither I can.
So can't I.

assessment.prompt: 'He passed the exam.' 'So ___ his brother.' (did / was)
Which sentence uses ellipsis?
options: She opened the door and walked in.
She opened the door and she walked in.
She opened the door and then she walked in.
assessment.why: The subject she is not repeated.

assessment.prompt: I like those shoes, but I prefer the black ___. (one / ones)
Which reply is correct? 'Is she coming?'
options: I don't think so.
I don't think not.
I think no.

lessons.title: Advanced reported speech
lessons.explain: Besides say and tell, English uses many reporting verbs that carry meaning: admit, deny, suggest, promise, warn, advise, accuse, apologise, insist, refuse. They are followed by different patterns: verb + to-infinitive, verb + object + to-infinitive, verb + -ing, or verb + that-clause. Tense does not always change if the statement is still true.
structures: Verb + to-infinitive: He promised to call. She refused to leave.
Verb + object + to-infinitive: She advised me to rest. He warned us not to go.
Verb + -ing: He admitted breaking it. She denied taking it. He suggested leaving.
positive: She advised me to apply for the job.
He admitted making a mistake.
They suggested meeting on Friday.
negative: He denied taking the money.
She warned us not to touch the wires.
questions: She asked whether I had finished.
He wondered if they would come.
reallife: Reporting a meeting: The manager promised to increase the budget.
Passing on advice: The doctor told me to avoid sugar.

mistakes.wrong: He suggested me to go.
mistakes.right: He suggested going. / He suggested that I go.
mistakes.why: Suggest is not followed by object + to-infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: She denied to take it.
mistakes.right: She denied taking it.
mistakes.why: Deny is followed by -ing.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She advised me to wait.
She advised me waiting.
She advised to wait me.

exercises.prompt: He admitted ___ the window. (break)
Report: 'I'll help you,' he said.
options: He promised to help me.
He promised helping me.
He promised me to helping.

exercises.prompt: She warned us not ___ the water. (to drink / drinking)

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He refused to pay.
He refused paying.
He refused for paying.

assessment.prompt: She apologised for ___ late. (be)
Report: 'Don't touch that!' she said to us.
options: She warned us not to touch it.
She warned us don't touch it.
She warned not touching us.

assessment.prompt: He denied ___ the money. (take)
Which is correct?
options: She suggested that we leave early.
She suggested us to leave early.
She suggested to us leave early.

lessons.title: Common grammatical errors
lessons.explain: Even advanced learners repeat certain mistakes. Knowing them helps you notice and correct them in your own speaking and writing. The most common are: confusing its and it's, their, there and they're, fewer and less, who and whom, misplaced modifiers, wrong prepositions and wrong tenses with time words.
structures: Fewer + countable: fewer people. Less + uncountable: less water.
Its (belonging to it) / it's (it is or it has).
Their (belonging to them) / there (place) / they're (they are).
positive: There are fewer cars on the road today.
They're going to sell their house.
The company changed its policy.
negative: I have less time than before.
It's not their fault.
questions: Who did you speak to? / To whom did you speak?
Is this their house or yours?
reallife: Emails: Please send me the report as soon as possible. (not ASAP in a formal letter)
Speaking: I am looking forward to seeing you.

mistakes.wrong: I am agree with you.
mistakes.right: I agree with you.
mistakes.why: Agree is a verb, so do not add am.

mistakes.wrong: There is less people here than yesterday.
mistakes.right: There are fewer people here than yesterday.
mistakes.why: People is countable, so use fewer, and the verb must be are.

mistakes.wrong: I have been living here since five years.
mistakes.right: I have been living here for five years.
mistakes.why: Use for with a period of time and since with a starting point.

Choose the correct sentence.

options: I am agree with you.
I agree with you.

options: Their going to be late.
They're going to be late.

Which sentence is correct?

Which is correct?

lessons.title: Causative structures
lessons.explain: A causative structure says that someone causes something to happen, or that you arrange for another person to do a job for you. Use have or get + object + past participle when someone else does the work: I had my car repaired. Use have + person + base verb, or get + person + to + verb, when you tell a person to do it: I had the mechanic check the brakes. Make, let and help are also causative verbs: She made me laugh. He let us go.
structures: Have/get + object + past participle: I had my hair cut. I got my phone fixed.
Have + person + base verb: I had the plumber fix the pipe.
Get + person + to + verb: I got my brother to help me.
Make/let + person + base verb: The teacher made us read.
positive: I had my house painted last month.
She is getting her passport renewed.
He got his friend to drive him home.
My boss made me work late.
negative: I didn't have my laptop repaired.
They won't let us enter without a ticket.
She didn't get anyone to help her.
questions: Where do you have your hair cut?
Have you had your eyes tested recently?
reallife: At a service centre: I would like to have my bike serviced.
At work: We are having the office painted next week.

mistakes.wrong: I repaired my phone at the shop.
mistakes.right: I had my phone repaired at the shop.
mistakes.why: You did not repair it yourself. Someone did it for you, so use have + object + past participle.

mistakes.wrong: She made me to laugh.
mistakes.right: She made me laugh.
mistakes.why: After make and let, use the base verb without to.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means someone else washed the car?
options: I had my car washed.
I washed my car.
I had washed my car.

exercises.prompt: She had her hair ___ yesterday. (cut)
The teacher made us ___ the poem. (learn)
exercises.why: After made, use the base verb.

exercises.prompt: Which means 'someone else will fix it'?
options: I will fix my bike.
I will get my bike fixed.
I will fix my bike myself.

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He let me to go.
He let me go.
He let me going.
assessment.why: After let, use the base verb without to.

assessment.prompt: We are going to have our house ___. (paint)
Which sentence is correct?
options: I got my brother help me.
I got my brother to help me.
I got my brother helping me.

assessment.prompt: She ___ her passport renewed last week. (have, past)
assessment.why: The past of have is had.

assessment.prompt: What does 'I had my eyes tested' mean?
options: Someone tested my eyes.
I tested someone's eyes.
I tested my own eyes.
assessment.why: Have + object + past participle means someone did it for you.

lessons.title: Advanced prepositions
lessons.explain: Many prepositions are fixed with certain words, so it helps to learn them in groups: adjective + preposition (afraid of, good at, interested in, keen on), verb + preposition (depend on, apologise for, consist of, succeed in) and noun + preposition (a reason for, an increase in, a solution to). Some pairs differ in meaning: in time means early enough, on time means exactly at the planned time; at the end is a point, in the end means finally. After a preposition use a noun or an -ing form: I am interested in learning.
structures: Adjective + preposition: She is afraid of dogs. He is good at maths.
Verb + preposition: It depends on the weather. He apologised for being late.
Noun + preposition: an increase in prices, a solution to the problem, a reason for the delay.
Preposition + -ing: She is interested in learning French.
positive: She is keen on photography.
The price of fuel has increased by ten per cent.
He succeeded in finding a job.
We arrived in time for the meeting.
negative: I am not afraid of exams.
He doesn't depend on anyone.
They didn't agree with the plan.
questions: What are you interested in?
Who is responsible for this project?
reallife: In an interview: I am very interested in this role and I am good at working in a team.
At work: We are looking for a solution to this problem.

mistakes.wrong: I am interested on music.
mistakes.right: I am interested in music.
mistakes.why: Interested is followed by in.

mistakes.wrong: She is good in English.
mistakes.right: She is good at English.
mistakes.why: Good is followed by at when we talk about a skill.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct preposition: She is afraid ___ spiders.
options: of
from
at

exercises.prompt: He apologised ___ being late. (for / to)
Which sentence is correct?
options: It depends of the weather.
It depends on the weather.
It depends in the weather.

exercises.prompt: There has been an increase ___ prices. (in / of)
exercises.why: We say an increase in prices.

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I am looking forward to meet you.
I am looking forward to meeting you.
I am looking forward for meeting you.
assessment.why: To here is a preposition, so use the -ing form.

assessment.prompt: She is very good ___ solving problems. (at / in)
Which one means 'early enough, before it is too late'?
options: on time
in time
at time
assessment.why: In time means early enough. On time means exactly at the planned time.

assessment.prompt: They congratulated me ___ passing the exam. (on / for)
Choose the correct sentence.
options: He is responsible of the project.
He is responsible for the project.
He is responsible to the project.

lessons.title: Formal and informal English
lessons.explain: Formal English is used at work, in study, in official letters and with people you do not know well. Informal English is used with friends and family and in casual messages. They differ in vocabulary (request or ask for, obtain or get), in grammar (contractions such as don't and phrasal verbs are common in informal speech) and in tone. Choose the style for your reader and the situation, and do not mix them. In a formal email use full forms and polite phrases, and avoid slang.
structures: Formal request: I would be grateful if you could send me the details.
Informal request: Can you send me the details?
Formal and informal verbs: request / ask for, purchase / buy, assist / help, commence / start.
positive: I would like to enquire about the position. (formal)
Hi, I wanted to ask about the job. (informal)
Please find the report attached. (formal)
Here is the report. (informal)
negative: I do not agree with this proposal. (formal)
I don't think that is a good idea. (informal)
questions: Could you please confirm the date of the meeting? (formal)
Can you tell me when the meeting is? (informal)
reallife: Email to a manager: Dear Mr Rao, I am writing to request a day of leave.
Message to a friend: Hey, can't make it today. Sorry!

mistakes.wrong: Dear Sir, Thanks a lot for ur help. See ya!
mistakes.right: Dear Sir, Thank you very much for your help. Kind regards.
mistakes.why: In a formal email use full words and a polite ending, with no slang or text spelling.

mistakes.wrong: Hey, I would be most grateful if you could kindly forward me the document at your earliest convenience.
mistakes.right: Hey, can you send me the document?
mistakes.why: Do not mix a very formal sentence with a casual greeting. Keep one style.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is more formal?
options: Can you help me?
Could you please assist me?
Help me, please.
exercises.why: Could you please assist me is polite and formal.

exercises.prompt: The formal word for 'buy' is ___. (purchase / get)
exercises.why: Purchase is the formal word for buy.

exercises.prompt: Which ending is best for a formal email?
options: See ya!
Kind regards
Bye bye
exercises.why: Kind regards is a polite, formal ending.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is informal?
options: I would be grateful for your reply.
Write back soon!
I look forward to hearing from you.
exercises.why: Write back soon is short and casual.

assessment.prompt: Which word is the formal word for 'start'?
options: begin
commence
kick off

assessment.prompt: Formal request: 'I would be ___ if you could reply soon.' (grateful / happy)
assessment.why: I would be grateful if you could is a polite formal request.

assessment.prompt: Which message suits a friend?
options: I wish to inform you that I shall be late.
I will be late, sorry!
Please be advised of my delay.
assessment.why: Short and friendly is right for a friend.

assessment.prompt: The formal word for 'get' (receive) is ___. (obtain / take)
assessment.why: Obtain is the formal word for get.

assessment.prompt: Which greeting suits an email to a company you do not know?
options: Hey guys,
Dear Sir or Madam,
Yo,
assessment.why: Dear Sir or Madam is formal.
